newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU CLEARS AID TO ALITALIA, IMPOSES CONDITIONS.
newsitem.headline: EU CLEARS AID TO ALITALIA, IMPOSES CONDITIONS.

text.p: The European Commission cleared payment of 2.75 trillion lire ($1.6 billion) in state-funded aid to Italian flag carrier Alitalia on Tuesday, imposing various conditions in return for approval.

Aid clearance, widely signalled in advance after the successful conclusion of negotiations between the Commission and the Rome government, included a requirement that the airline sell its holding in the Hungarian carrier MALEV, a statement said.

Payment of the aid will come in three instalments of two trillion, 500 billion and 250 billion lire respectively, the first due immediately and including one trillion already paid in June 1996, the statement added.
"The remainder will be conditional on the satisfactory progress of the company's restructuring plan and on the respect of a series of conditions," the statement said.

"This decision should close the cycle of state aid applications that has characterised the efforts by European airlines to restructure and meet the challenges of global competition," European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said in the statement.

"Practically all European carriers have made radical internal changes in recent years," Kinnock said, a reference to a series of aid clearances in which has seen cash injections to Spain's Iberia , Air France , TAP Air Portugal, Greece's Olympic Airways and Ireland's Aer Lingus .
"In the future the Commission's role will, accordingly, move away from the scrutiny of capital injections to considerations of the terms of conditions of mergers and alliances," he added.
That said, Commission officials are still in talks with Athens over the release of aid which was frozen after alleged abuses of approval conditions for Olympic's 1994 aid package.
Tuesday's decision follows drawn-out talks between Rome and Brussels since June 1996, when the airline posted its planned restructuring and funding plans for scrutiny.
The Commission rejected the Italian state's contention that the cash injection mirrored the behaviour of a normal investor, saying it payment should be treated as state aid under EU law.

That prompted Alitalia to offer to cut 27,000 flights a year from its timetables, abandon fleet expansion plans, cut staff numbers by 1,212 between 1996 and 2000 and sell its stake in the computer reservation system GALILEO.

Further concessions secured by the Commission included a promise from authorities to behave as "normal shareholders" in relations with Alitalia and to refrain from giving further subsidy in the form of loan guarantees.
Nor could authorities prefer Alitalia over other EU carriers in the allocation of traffic rights, take-off and landing slots, ground-handling services and access to airport infrastructures.
Other conditions forbid Alitalia from using its new money to buy into other carriers and bar it from undercutting its competitors' fares until the end of 2000.
